1
開元九年，麟德曆署日蝕比不效，詔僧一行作新曆，推大衍數立術以應之，較經史所書氣朔、日名、宿度可考者皆合。 十五年，草成而一行卒，詔特進張說與曆官陳玄景等次為曆術七篇、略例一篇、曆議十篇，玄宗顧訪者則稱制旨。 明年，說表上之，起十七年頒于有司。 時善算瞿曇譔者，怨不得預改曆事，二十一年，與玄景奏：「大衍寫九執曆，其術未盡。 」太子右司禦率南宮說亦非之。 詔侍御史李麟、太史令桓執圭較靈臺候簿，大衍十得七、八，麟德纔三、四，九執一、二焉。 乃罪說等，而是否決。
In Kaiyuan 9 (721), the Linde calendar's predicted solar eclipses failed to match observation. The throne ordered the monk Yixing to compile a new calendar: he worked out the Dayan numerology, set up the computational procedures to match heaven, and checked every verifiable entry in the classics and histories for qi and new moons, day designations, and lodge positions—they all agreed. In Kaiyuan 15 the draft was finished, but Yixing died before it could be promulgated. The court ordered Senior Grand Master Zhang Yue, the calendar officer Chen Xuanjing, and others to edit the work into seven chapters of calendrical method, one chapter of summary principles, and ten chapters of calendrical discourse; passages that reflected Emperor Xuanzong's own inquiries were labeled as bearing the imperial directive. The following year Zhang Yue submitted it in a memorial, and from Kaiyuan 17 onward it was distributed to the responsible bureaus. Gautama Siddha, a master calculator, had been shut out of the reform and bore a grudge. In Kaiyuan 21 he joined Chen Xuanjing in a memorial: 'The Dayan calendar merely copies the Indian Navagraha system; its methods are still incomplete.' ' Nangong Shuo, Right Assistant Director in the Crown Prince's Palace Guard, likewise attacked the calendar. The throne ordered Attending Censor Li Lin and Observatory Director Huan Zhigui to test the calendars against the Spirit Terrace observation logs. The Dayan system matched seven or eight predictions in ten; the Linde only three or four; the Navagraha barely one or two. Nangong Shuo and his allies were punished, and the challenge was rejected.
2
自太初至麟德，曆有二十三家，與天雖近而未密也。 至一行，密矣，其倚數立法固無以易也。 後世雖有改作者，皆依倣而已，故詳錄之。 略例，所以明述作本旨也； 曆議，所以考古今得失也。 其說皆足以為將來折衷。 略其大要，著于篇者十有二。
From the Taichu calendar down to the Linde, twenty-three systems had been used; each approached the heavens closely, yet none was truly precise. Yixing's calendar achieved precision; because its laws were grounded in number, nothing could supplant it. Later reformers only followed his model, which is why this treatise records it at length. The summary principles explain the author's original purpose; the calendar discourse weighs the successes and failures of earlier and current systems. Both bodies of argument are fit to guide future adjudication. The essentials are distilled into twelve main topics in what follows.
3
其一曆本議曰：
The first topic, the discourse on calendrical foundations, reads:
4
易：「天數五，地數五，五位相得而各有合，所以成變化而行鬼神也。 」天數始於一，地數始於二，合二始以位剛柔。 天數終於九，地數終於十，合二終以紀閏餘。 天數中於五，地數中於六，合二中以通律曆。 天有五音，所以司日也。 地有六律，所以司辰也。 參伍相周，究於六十，聖人以此見天地之心也。 自五以降，為五行生數； 自六以往，為五材成數。 錯而乘之，以生數衍成位。 一、六而退極，五、十而增極； 一、六為爻位之統，五、十為大衍之母。 成數乘生數，其算六百，為天中之積。 生數乘成數，其算亦六百，為地中之積。 合千有二百，以五十約之，則四象周六爻也； 二十四約之，則太極包四十九用也。 綜成數，約中積，皆十五。 綜生數，約中積，皆四十。 兼而為天地之數，以五位取之，復得二中之合矣。 蓍數之變，九、六各一，乾坤之象也。 七、八各三，六子之象也。 故爻數通乎六十，策數行乎二百四十。 是以大衍為天地之樞，如環之無端，蓋律曆之大紀也。
The Book of Changes says: 'Heaven's number is five and earth's number is five; the five positions pair off and each finds its match—by this change is wrought and the work of spirits and ghosts is carried out.' ' Heaven's counting begins at one, earth's at two; combining these two starting points fixes the places of yin and yang. Heaven's counting ends at nine, earth's at ten; joining the two endings registers the intercalary surplus. Heaven's mean lies at five, earth's at six; joining these two means links pitch pipes with the calendar. Heaven has the five tones, and through them it governs the day. Earth has the six pitch pipes, and through them it governs the hours. Three and five cycle together until they reach sixty—the sage reads in this the mind of heaven and earth. From five downward lie the generating numbers of the five phases; from six upward lie the completion numbers of the five materials. Interwoven and multiplied, the generating numbers unfold into positional values. One and six mark the retreating pole, five and ten the advancing pole; one and six govern the lines of the hexagrams, five and ten are the mother-numbers of the Great Expansion. When completion numbers multiply generating numbers the product is six hundred—the accumulated value at heaven's center. When generating numbers multiply completion numbers the product is likewise six hundred—the accumulated value at earth's center. Together they make twelve hundred; divided by fifty, this yields the four images cycling through the six lines; divided by twenty-four, the Supreme Pole enfolds the forty-nine stalks put to use. Summing the completion numbers and reducing the central accumulations, each yields fifteen. Summing the generating numbers and reducing the central accumulations, each yields forty. Combined as the numbers of heaven and earth and taken by the five positions, one again arrives at the union of the two means. In the changes of the yarrow stalks, nine and six each appear once—the images of Qian and Kun. Seven and eight each appear three times—the images of the six derived trigrams. Thus the line numbers run through sixty, and the stalk counts through two hundred forty. Great Expansion is therefore the pivot of heaven and earth, endless as a ring—the grand charter of pitch pipes and calendar alike.
5
夫數象微於三、四，而章於七、八。 卦有三微，策有四象，故二微之合，在始中之際焉。 蓍以七備，卦以八周，故二章之合，而在中終之際焉。 中極居五六間，由闢闔之交，而在章微之際者，人神之極也。 天地中積，千有二百，揲之以四，為爻率三百； 以十位乘之，而二章之積三千； 以五材乘八象，為二微之積四十。 兼章微之積，則氣朔之分母也。 以三極參之，倍六位除之，凡七百六十，是謂辰法，而齊於代軌。 以十位乘之，倍大衍除之，凡三百四，是謂刻法，而齊于德運。 半氣朔之母，千五百二十，得天地出符之數，因而三之，凡四千五百六十，當七精返初之會也。 易始于三微而生一象，四象成而後八卦章。 三變皆剛，太陽之象。 三變皆柔，太陰之象。 一剛二柔，少陽之象。 一柔二剛，少陰之象。 少陽之剛，有始、有壯、有究。 少陰之柔，有始、有壯、有究。 兼三才而兩之，神明動乎其中。 故四十九象，而大業之用周矣。 數之德圓，故紀之以三而變於七。 象之德方，故紀之以四而變于八。
Number and image are subtle at three and four, but fully expressed at seven and eight. The hexagram holds three subtleties and the stalks four images; the joining of two subtleties therefore falls at the boundary between beginning and center. The stalks are complete at seven, the hexagrams cycle at eight; the joining of two chapters therefore falls at the boundary between center and end. The central pole lies between five and six, born where opening meets closing and standing where chapter meets subtlety—this is the utmost of humanity and the divine. The central accumulation of heaven and earth is twelve hundred; counted out by fours, this gives the line rate of three hundred; multiplied by the ten positions, the accumulation of two chapters is three thousand; the five materials multiplied by eight images yield the accumulation of two subtleties: forty. Adding the accumulations of chapter and subtlety gives the denominator for qi and new moon. Cross-checked with the three poles, doubled, and divided by the six positions, the total is seven hundred sixty—this is the double-hour divisor, aligned with the generational cycle. Multiplied by the ten positions, doubled, and divided by the Great Expansion constant, the total is three hundred four—this is the quarter divisor, aligned with the virtue cycle. Half the qi-and-new-moon base is fifteen hundred twenty; this yields the number by which heaven and earth issue their tally. Tripled, it becomes four thousand five hundred sixty—the epoch when the seven luminaries return to their starting points. The Changes start from three subtleties to produce one image; once the four images are complete, the eight trigrams stand revealed. Three changes all yielding yang lines—the image of great yang. Three changes all yielding yin lines—the image of great yin. One yang and two yin—the image of lesser yang. One yin and two yang—the image of lesser yin. Within lesser yang, each yang line has its beginning, its fullness, and its completion. Within lesser yin, each yin line has its beginning, its fullness, and its completion. Embracing the three powers and doubling them, the spirits stir within. Thus the forty-nine images, and the great work of the Changes runs its full course. Number's nature is circular, so it is recorded in threes and transforms at seven. Image's nature is square, so it is recorded in fours and transforms at eight.
6
人在天地中，以閱盈虛之變，則閏餘之初，而氣朔所虛也。 以終合通大衍之母，虧其地十，凡九百四十為通數。 終合除之，得中率四十九，餘十九分之九，終歲之弦，而斗分復初之朔也。 地於終極之際，虧十而從天，所以遠疑陽之戰也。 夫十九分之九，盈九而虛十也。 乾盈九，隱乎龍戰之中，故不見其首。 坤虛十，以導潛龍之氣，故不見其成。 周日之朔分，周歲之閏分，與一章之弦，一蔀之月，皆合於九百四十，蓋取諸中率也。
Human beings stand between heaven and earth to watch fullness and emptiness shift; the origin of the intercalary surplus is the void through which qi and new moon pass. Linking the terminal union to the mother of Great Expansion and deducting earth's ten yields nine hundred forty as the universal divisor. Dividing by the end-union gives a central rate of forty-nine with a remainder of nine parts in nineteen—the year's final quarter-moon, when the Dipper fraction returns to the opening new moon. At the ultimate juncture earth sheds ten and follows heaven, keeping at bay the feared clash of yang forces. Nine parts in nineteen means fullness at nine and emptiness at ten. Qian fills at nine and hides within the dragon's battle, so its head is not seen. Kun empties at ten to channel the hidden dragon's breath, so its completion is not seen. The new-moon fraction of the weekly cycle, the intercalary fraction of the yearly cycle, one chapter's quarter-moon, and one obscuration's month—all converge on nine hundred forty, drawn from the central rate.
7
一策之分十九，而章法生； 一揲之分七十六，而蔀法生。 一蔀之日二萬七千七百五十七，以通數約之，凡二十九日餘四百九十九，而日月相及於朔，此六爻之紀也。 以卦當歲，以爻當月，以策當日，凡三十二歲而小終，二百八十五小終而與卦運大終，二百八十五，則參伍二終之合也。 數象既合，而遯行之變在乎其間矣。
One stalk's fraction is nineteen, from which the chapter divisor arises; one counting-out's fraction is seventy-six, from which the obscuration divisor arises. An obscuration contains twenty-seven thousand seven hundred fifty-seven days; reduced by the universal divisor this is twenty-nine days with a remainder of four hundred ninety-nine—the interval in which sun and moon meet at new moon, the measure of the six lines. The hexagram stands for the year, the line for the month, the stalk for the day: thirty-two years form a small cycle; two hundred eighty-five small cycles complete the hexagram's great cycle—two hundred eighty-five being the union of the paired three-and-five completions. Once number and image are aligned, the shifts of hidden transit unfold between them.
8
所謂遯行者，以爻率乘朔餘，為十四萬九千七百，以四十九用、二十四象虛之，復以爻率約之，為四百九十八、微分七十五太半，則章微之中率也。 二十四象，象有四十九蓍，凡千一百七十六。 故虛遯之數七十三，半氣朔之母，以三極乘參伍，以兩儀乘二十四變，因而幷之，得千六百一十三，為朔餘。 四揲氣朔之母，以八氣九精遯其十七，得七百四十三，為氣餘。 歲八萬九千七百七十三而氣朔會，是謂章率。 歲二億七千二百九十萬九百二十而無小餘，合于夜半，是謂蔀率。 歲百六十三億七千四百五十九萬五千二百而大餘與歲建俱終，是謂元率。 此不易之道也。
Hidden transit means: multiply the new-moon remainder by the line rate to obtain one hundred forty-nine thousand seven hundred; subtract the forty-nine uses and twenty-four images; reduce again by the line rate to four hundred ninety-eight with a fine fraction of seventy-five and a half—the central rate between chapter and subtlety. Twenty-four images, each with forty-nine stalks, total one thousand one hundred seventy-six. The void for hidden transit is therefore seventy-three. Half the qi-and-new-moon base, multiplied by the three poles and by three-and-five, the two regulators by twenty-four changes, then combined, gives one thousand six hundred thirteen as the new-moon remainder. Four countings of the qi-and-new-moon base, with the eight qi and nine luminaries in hidden transit deducting seventeen, yield seven hundred forty-three as the qi remainder. At eighty-nine thousand seven hundred seventy-three per year qi and new moon coincide—this is the chapter rate. At two hundred seventy-two million nine hundred thousand nine hundred twenty per year with no small remainder, aligning at midnight—this is the obscuration rate. At sixteen billion three hundred seventy-four million five hundred ninety-five thousand two hundred per year the great remainder and the year's establishment both terminate—this is the origin rate. This is the unchanging principle.
9
策以紀日，象以紀月。 故乾坤之策三百六十，為日度之準。 乾坤之用四十九象，為月弦之檢。 日之一度，不盈全策； 月之一弦，不盈全用。 故策餘萬五千九百四十三，則十有二中所盈也。 用差萬七千一百二十四，則十有二朔所虛也。 綜盈虛之數，五歲而再閏。 中節相距，皆當三五； 弦望相距，皆當二七。 升降之應，發斂之候，皆紀之以策而從日者也。 表裏之行，朓朒之變，皆紀之以用而從月者也。
Stalks tally the day; images tally the month. The stalk counts of Qian and Kun total three hundred sixty—the standard for the sun's daily motion. The forty-nine images put to use in Qian and Kun are the gauge for the moon's phases. One degree of the sun's motion does not fill a whole stalk count; one lunar phase does not exhaust a whole stalk use. Hence the stalk remainder of fifteen thousand nine hundred forty-three is what the twelve centers overflow. The use difference of seventeen thousand one hundred twenty-four is what the twelve new moons leave void. Combining fullness and emptiness, an intercalary month is inserted every five years. Mid-season nodes are spaced at intervals of three and five; first and full moons are spaced at intervals of two and seven. The rhythms of ascent and descent, the markers of issuing and gathering—all are recorded by stalk counts and follow the sun. The inner and outer courses, the shifts between crescent and gibbous—all are recorded by stalk uses and follow the moon.
10
積算曰演紀，日法曰通法，月氣曰中朔，朔實曰揲法，歲分曰策實，周天曰乾實，餘分曰虛分。 氣策曰三元，一元之策，則天一遯行也。 月策曰四象，一象之策，則朔、弦、望相距也。 五行用事，曰發斂。 候策曰天中，卦策曰地中，半卦曰貞悔。 旬周曰爻數，小分母曰象統。 日行曰躔，其差曰盈縮，積盈縮曰先後。 古者平朔，月朝見曰朒，夕見曰朓。 今以日之所盈縮、月之所遲疾損益之，或進退其日，以為定朔。 舒亟之度，乃數使然，躔離相錯，偕以損益，故同謂之朓朒。 月行曰離，遲疾曰轉度，母曰轉法。 遲疾有衰，其變者勢也。 月逶迤馴屈，行不中道，進退遲速，不率其常。 過中則為速，不及中則為遲。 積遲謂之屈，積速謂之伸。 陽，執中以出令，故曰先後； 陰，含章以聽命，故曰屈伸。 日不及中則損之，過則益之。 月不及中則益之，過則損之。 尊卑之用睽，而及中之志同。 觀晷景之進退，知軌道之升降。 軌與晷名舛而義合，其差則水漏之所從也。 總名曰軌漏。 中晷長短謂之陟降。 景長則夜短，景短則夜長。 積其陟降，謂之消息。 遊交曰交會，交而周曰交終。 交終不及朔，謂之朔差。 交中不及望，謂之望差。 日道表曰陽曆，其裏曰陰曆。 五星見伏周，謂之終率。 以分從日謂之終日，其差為進退。
Accumulated calculation is termed evolving era; the day divisor is the universal method; month and qi together are central new moon; new-moon substance is the counting method; the year's fraction is stalk substance; the circuit of heaven is Qian substance; the remainder fraction is the void fraction. Qi stalks are called the three origins; one origin's stalk count is heaven-one in hidden transit. Month stalks are called the four images; one image's stalk count is the interval from new moon through quarter to full. The periods when the five phases hold sway are termed issuing and gathering. Period stalks are heaven's center; hexagram stalks are earth's center; half a hexagram is correct and regret. The ten-day cycle is the line number; the small denominator is the image norm. The sun's daily motion is called transit; its deviation is excess and deficit; accumulated excess and deficit is termed advance and retard. In antiquity calendars used mean new moons; when the moon appeared in the morning it was called the waning crescent, and when it appeared in the evening, the waxing crescent. Now we adjust by the sun's apogee-perigee variation and the moon's anomaly of motion, advancing or retreating the date as needed, and thus obtain the true new moon. Slow and fast degrees arise from numerical calculation; lunar transit degrees interact and offset each other, and both are adjusted together—hence they are jointly termed waxing and waning crescents. The moon's motion is termed li; its anomaly of slow and fast motion is rotation degrees; the divisor is the rotation method. The anomaly of motion has a declining phase; what actually varies is its momentum. The moon's path winds and bends; it does not travel the mean course, and its progress and retreat, slow and fast phases, do not follow a fixed rate. When it passes the mean point it is fast; when it falls short of the mean point it is slow. Accumulated slowness is termed contraction; accumulated speed is termed extension. Yang holds the center to issue commands, and so is called earlier and later; Yin embraces its pattern to receive commands, and so is called contraction and extension. When the sun falls short of the mean, subtract; when it passes the mean, add. When the moon falls short of the mean, add; when it passes the mean, subtract. Their roles as superior and inferior differ, yet their aim of reaching the mean is the same. By observing the advance and retreat of the gnomon shadow, one knows the rise and fall of the solar path. Orbit and gnomon differ in name but agree in meaning; their discrepancy is what the water clepsydra measures. Together they are called orbit and clepsydra. The length and shortness of the noon gnomon shadow is termed ascent and descent. When the shadow is long, the night is short; when the shadow is short, the night is long. Accumulating these ascents and descents is termed waxing and waning. A wandering crossing is called conjunction; when the crossing completes a cycle it is called conjunction completion. When conjunction completion falls short of new moon, it is called new-moon discrepancy. When the crossing at midpoint falls short of full moon, it is called full-moon discrepancy. The outer side of the sun's path is the yang calendar; its inner side is the yin calendar. The cycle of visibility and concealment of the five planets is called the terminal ratio. Following the sun by fractional parts is the terminal day; the discrepancy becomes advance and retreat.
11
其二中氣議曰：
The second discourse, on mid-qi, states:
12
曆氣始于冬至，稽其實，蓋取諸晷景。 春秋傳僖公五年正月辛亥朔，日南至。 以周曆推之，入壬子蔀第四章，以辛亥一分合朔冬至，殷曆則壬子蔀首也。 昭公二十年二月己丑朔，日南至。 魯史失閏，至不在正。 左氏記之，以懲司曆之罪。 周曆得己丑二分，殷曆得庚寅一分。 殷曆南至常在十月晦，則中氣後天也。 周曆蝕朔差經或二日，則合朔先天也。 傳所據者周曆也，緯所據者殷曆也。 氣合于傳，朔合于緯，斯得之矣。 戊寅曆月氣專合于緯，麟德曆專合于傳，偏取之，故兩失之。 又命曆序以為孔子脩春秋用殷曆，使其數可傳於後。 考其蝕朔不與殷曆合，及開元十二年，朔差五日矣，氣差八日矣。 上不合於經，下不足以傳於後代，蓋哀、平間治甲寅元曆者託之，非古也。 又漢太史令張壽王說黃帝調曆以非太初。 有司劾：「官有黃帝調曆不與壽王同，壽王所治乃殷曆也。 」漢自中興以來，圖讖漏泄，而考靈曜、命曆序皆有甲寅元，其所起在四分曆庚申元後百一十四歲。 延光初中謁者亶誦，靈帝時五官郎中馮光等，皆請用之，卒不施行。 緯所載壬子冬至，則其遺術也。 魯曆南至，又先周曆四分日之三，而朔後九百四十分日之五十一。 故僖公五年辛亥為十二月晦，壬子為正月朔。 又推日蝕密於殷曆，其以閏餘一為章首，亦取合於當時也。
Calendar qi begins at the winter solstice; examining the facts, it fundamentally derives from gnomon observations. The Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals records that on the new moon of the first month of Duke Xi's fifth year (xinhai day), the sun reached its southern extreme—the winter solstice. Reckoned by the Zhou calendar, one enters the fourth chapter of the renzi obscuration cycle, with xinhai day and a one-part fraction for conjunction and winter solstice on the same day; in the Yin calendar, renzi is the obscuration head. In Duke Zhao's twentieth year, on the new moon of the second month (jichou day), the sun again reached its southern extreme. The Lu chronicle missed an intercalary month, and the solstice did not fall in the proper first month. Zuo Qiuming recorded the fact to expose the calendar officers' error. The Zhou calendar yields jichou with a two-part fraction; the Yin calendar yields gengyin with a one-part fraction. In the Yin calendar the solstice constantly fell on the last day of the tenth month, so the mid-qi terms lagged behind heaven. In the Zhou calendar the new-moon discrepancy for eclipses sometimes reached two days, so conjunction fell ahead of heaven. The Commentary relies on the Zhou calendar, while the Apocrypha rely on the Yin calendar. Match qi to the Commentary and new moons to the Apocrypha—that is how to get it right. The Wuyin calendar matched month and qi only to the Apocrypha, and the Linde calendar only to the Commentary; by taking either side alone, both missed the mark. The Command Calendar Preface further claims that Confucius edited the Spring and Autumn using the Yin calendar so its numbers could be handed down to posterity. Yet when eclipse dates and new moons are checked against the Yin calendar they do not agree; by Kaiyuan 12 the new-moon error had grown to five days and the qi error to eight. It fails to match the classics above and cannot be credibly handed down below; the claim was likely forged by compilers of the jiayin-origin calendar in the Ai-Ping period—it is not ancient tradition. The Han Grand Astrologer Zhang Shouwang also invoked the Yellow Emperor's Harmonized Calendar to criticize the Taichu system. The authorities impeached him: "The official Yellow Emperor Harmonized Calendar differs from Shouwang's version—what Shouwang actually used was the Yin calendar. " After the Han restoration, prognostic charts and apocryphal texts circulated openly, and both the Investigating the Luminous Radiance and the Command Calendar Preface posit a jiayin origin, beginning 114 years after the gengshen origin of the Quarter-Remainder calendar. In the early Yan'guang era, Palace Attendant Dan Song, and under Emperor Ling the Five-Offices Court Gentleman Feng Guang and others all petitioned to adopt it, but it was never put into practice. The renzi winter solstice recorded in the Apocrypha represents the surviving method of that tradition. The Lu calendar's solstice fell three-quarters of a day earlier than the Zhou calendar's, while its new moon lagged by fifty-one parts in nine hundred and forty parts of a day. Accordingly, in Duke Xi's fifth year xinhai was the last day of the twelfth month, and renzi was the new moon of the first month. Eclipses also compute more closely by the Yin calendar; its use of an intercalation remainder of one for the chapter head likewise sought agreement with conditions of that era.
13
開元十二年十一月，陽城測景，以癸未極長，較其前後所差，則夜半前尚有餘分。 新曆大餘十九，加時九十九刻，而皇極、戊寅、麟德曆皆得甲申，以玄始曆氣分二千四百四十三為率，推而上之，則失春秋辛亥，是減分太多也。 以皇極曆氣分二千四百四十五為率，推而上之，雖合春秋，而失元嘉十九年乙巳冬至及開皇五年甲戌冬至、七年癸未夏至； 若用麟德曆率二千四百四十七，又失春秋己丑。 是減分太少也。 故新曆以二千四百四十四為率，而舊所失者皆中矣。
In the eleventh month of Kaiyuan 12, Yang Cheng measured shadows and found guiwei day at maximum length; comparing the discrepancy before and after, there were still fractional parts remaining before midnight. The new calendar yields a great remainder of nineteen and an hour-addition of ninety-nine ke, while the Huangji, Wuyin, and Linde calendars all give jiashen; projecting upward at the Xuanshi calendar's qi fraction of 2443 misses the Spring and Autumn xinhai date—too many parts were subtracted. Using the Huangji calendar's qi fraction of 2445 and projecting backward matches the Spring and Autumn dates but misses the winter solstice of Yuanjia 19 (yisi), the winter solstice of Kaihuang 5 (jiaxu), and the summer solstice of Kaihuang 7 (guimei); If the Linde rate of 2447 is used, the Spring and Autumn jichou date is missed instead. Too few parts were subtracted. The new calendar therefore adopts 2444 as its rate, and every date the older systems missed is now matched.
14
漢會稽東部尉劉洪以四分疎闊，由斗分多。 更以五百八十九為紀法，百四十五為斗分，減餘太甚，是以不及四十年而加時漸覺先天。 韓翊、楊偉、劉智等皆稍損益，更造新術，而皆依讖緯「三百歲改憲」之文，考經之合朔多中，較傳之南至則否。 玄始曆以為十九年七閏，皆有餘分，是以中氣漸差。 據渾天，二分為東西之中，而晷景不等； 二至為南北之極，而進退不齊。 此古人所未達也。 更因劉洪紀法，增十一年以為章歲，而減閏餘十九分之一。 春秋後五十四年，歲在甲寅，直應鍾章首，與景初曆閏餘皆盡。 雖減章閏，然中氣加時尚差，故未合于春秋。 其斗分幾得中矣。
Liu Hong, Eastern Commandant of Kuaiji in Han times, found the Quarter-Remainder calendar too coarse—because its dipper fraction was too large. He set 589 as the era divisor and 145 as the dipper fraction, reducing the remainder too drastically; within forty years the computed hour-addition was already noticeably ahead of heaven. Han Yi, Yang Wei, Liu Zhi, and others each made minor adjustments and devised new methods, all invoking the apocryphal dictum that "the statute is reformed every three hundred years"; their conjunction dates mostly matched the classics, but their solstice dates did not match the Commentary. The Xuanshi calendar treated each nineteen-year, seven-intercalation cycle as retaining fractional remainders, so the mid-qi terms gradually drifted. On the armillary-sphere model, the equinoxes mark the east-west midpoint, yet noon shadows at those points are unequal; The solstices mark the north-south extremes, yet the advance and retreat of shadows do not align evenly. This the ancients had not understood. Building on Liu Hong's era divisor, eleven years were added to the chapter length and the intercalation remainder was reduced by one-nineteenth. Fifty-four years after the Spring and Autumn era, in the jiayin year, the cycle directly aligned with the zhong chapter head, and the intercalation remainders matched those of the Jingchu calendar exactly. Although the chapter intercalation was reduced, the hour-addition for mid-qi still missed the mark, and so it did not match the Spring and Autumn records. Its dipper fraction was nearly right.
15
後代曆家，皆因循玄始，而損益或過差。 大抵古曆未減斗分，其率自二千五百以上。 乾象至于元嘉曆，未減閏餘，其率自二千四百六十以上。 玄始、大明至麟德曆皆減分破章，其率自二千四百二十九以上。 較前代史官注記，惟元嘉十三年十一月甲戌景長，皇極、麟德、開元曆皆得癸酉，蓋日度變常爾。 祖沖之既失甲戌冬至，以為加時太早，增小餘以附會之。 而十二年戊辰景長，得己巳； 十七年甲午景長，得乙未； 十八年己亥景長，得庚子。 合一失三，其失愈多。 劉孝孫、張冑玄因之，小餘益強，又以十六年己丑景長為庚寅矣。 治曆者糾合眾同，以稽其所異，苟獨異焉，則失行可知。 今曲就其一，而少者失三，多者失五，是捨常數而從失行也。 周建德六年，以壬辰景長，而麟德、開元曆皆得癸巳。 開皇七年，以癸未景短，而麟德、開元曆皆得壬午。 先後相戾，不可叶也，皆日行盈縮使然。
Later calendar makers all followed the Xuanshi system, but their adjustments sometimes overshot. Broadly speaking, ancient calendars that had not reduced the dipper fraction had rates of 2500 or higher. From the Qianxiang calendar through the Yuanjia calendar, those that had not reduced the intercalation remainder had rates of 2460 or higher. The Xuanshi, Daming, and down to the Linde calendars all reduced fractions and broke chapter cycles, with rates of 2429 or higher. Comparing annotated records of past dynasties' historiographers, only for the long shadow on jiaxu day of the eleventh month of Yuanjia 13 do the Huangji, Linde, and Kaiyuan calendars all give guiyou—likely because the sun's apparent motion varied from its usual rate. Zu Chongzhi, having missed the jiaxu winter solstice, assumed the hour-addition was too early and increased the small remainder to force a fit. Yet for the long shadow in year 12 (wuchen), his calendar gives jisi; For year 17 (jiawu), the long shadow yields yiwei; For year 18 (jihai), the long shadow yields gengzi. One match against three misses—the errors multiply. Liu Xiaosun and Zhang Zhouxuan followed suit, strengthening the small remainder further, and likewise shifted the long shadow of year 16 (jichou) to gengyin. Calendar makers collate shared results to check discrepancies; where a system stands alone, its error is evident. Now, by forcing agreement with one outlier—three misses at best, five at worst—they abandon the constant rate to follow aberrant motion. In the sixth year of Jiande in Northern Zhou, the observed long shadow fell on renchen day, yet the Linde and Kaiyuan calendars both give guisi. In Kaihuang 7 the short shadow was on guimei day, yet the Linde and Kaiyuan calendars both give renwu. The discrepancies in sequence cannot be reconciled—they all stem from the sun's variation in daily motion.
16
凡曆術在於常數，而不在於變行。 既叶中行之率，則可以兩齊先後之變矣。 麟德已前，實錄所記，乃依時曆書之，非候景所得。 又比年候景，長短不均，由加時有早晏，行度有盈縮也。
Calendrical method depends on constant rates, not on variable motion. Once the mean motion rate is correct, both kinds of advance-and-retreat variation can be reconciled. Before the Linde calendar, entries in the Veritable Records were taken from the calendar then in use, not from gnomon observations. Moreover, recent gnomon observations show uneven shadow lengths because the computed hour-addition varies early or late and the sun's traveled degrees expand and contract.
17
自春秋以來，至開元十二年，冬、夏至凡三十一事，戊寅曆得十六，麟德曆得二十三，開元曆得二十四。
From the Spring and Autumn period through Kaiyuan 12, there are thirty-one recorded winter and summer solstices; the Wuyin calendar matches sixteen, the Linde twenty-three, and the Kaiyuan twenty-four.
18
其三合朔議曰：
The third discourse, on conjunction for new moon, states:
19
日月合度謂之朔。 無所取之，取之蝕也。 春秋日蝕有甲乙者三十四。 殷曆、魯曆先一日者十三，後一日者三； 周曆先一日者二十二，先二日者九。 其偽可知矣。
When sun and moon reach the same degree, it is called new moon. With no direct means of verification, one verifies by eclipses. The Spring and Autumn Annals record thirty-four solar eclipses with day designations in the jia-yi cycle. Against the Yin and Lu calendars, thirteen eclipses appear one day early and three one day late; Against the Zhou calendar, twenty-two appear one day early and nine two days early. Its unreliability is obvious.
20
莊公三十年九月庚午朔，襄公二十一年九月庚戌朔，定公五年三月辛亥朔，當以盈縮、遲速為定朔。 殷曆雖合，適然耳，非正也。 僖公五年正月辛亥朔，十二月丙子朔，十四年三月己丑朔； 文公元年五月辛酉朔，十一年三月甲申晦； 襄公十九年五月壬辰晦； 昭公元年十二月甲辰朔，二十年二月己丑朔，二十三年正月壬寅朔、七月戊辰晦：皆與周曆合。 其所記多周、齊、晉事，蓋周王所頒，齊、晉用之。 僖公十五年九月己卯晦，十六年正月戊申朔； 成公十六年六月甲午晦； 襄公十八年十月丙寅晦、十一月丁卯朔，二十六年三月甲寅朔，二十七年六月丁未朔：與殷曆、魯曆合。 此非合蝕，故仲尼因循時史，而所記多宋、魯事，與齊、晉不同可知矣。
The new moons on gengwu day of the ninth month in Duke Zhuang's thirtieth year, gengxu day of the ninth month in Duke Xiang's twenty-first year, and xinhai day of the third month in Duke Ding's fifth year should all be treated as true new moons adjusted for solar and lunar anomaly. That the Yin calendar happens to agree is mere coincidence, not proof of correctness. The new moons on xinhai in the first month of Duke Xi's fifth year, bingzi in the twelfth month, and jichou in the third month of his fourteenth year; Xinyou in the fifth month of Duke Wen's first year, and the last day of the third month (jiashen) in his eleventh year; The last day of the fifth month (renchen) in Duke Xiang's nineteenth year; Jiachen in the twelfth month of Duke Zhao's first year, jichou in the second month of his twentieth year, and renyin new moon in the first month and wuchen last day in the seventh month of his twenty-third year—all agree with the Zhou calendar. Its entries chiefly concern Zhou, Qi, and Jin; presumably the Zhou king issued it and Qi and Jin adopted it. The last day of the ninth month (jimao) in Duke Xi's fifteenth year, and the new moon of the first month (wushen) in his sixteenth year; The last day of the sixth month (jiawu) in Duke Cheng's sixteenth year; The last day of the tenth month (bingyin) and the new moon of the eleventh month (dingmao) in Duke Xiang's eighteenth year, the new moon of the third month (jiayin) in his twenty-sixth year, and the new moon of the sixth month (dingwei) in his twenty-seventh year—all agree with the Yin and Lu calendars. These dates do not match eclipses; Confucius simply followed the chronicles of his day. That his records chiefly concern Song and Lu—not Qi and Jin—is therefore plain.
21
昭公十二年十月壬申朔，原輿人逐原伯絞，與魯曆、周曆皆差一日，此丘明即其所聞書之也。 僖公二十二年十一月己巳朔，宋、楚戰于泓。 周、殷、魯曆皆先一日，楚人所赴也。 昭公二十年六月丁巳晦，衞侯與北宮喜盟； 七月戊午朔，遂盟國人。 三曆皆先二日，衞人所赴也。 此則列國之曆不可以一術齊矣。 而長曆日子不在其月，則改易閏餘，欲以求合。 故閏月相距，近則十餘月，遠或七十餘月，此杜預所甚繆也。 夫合朔先天，則經書日蝕以糾之。 中氣後天，則傳書南至以明之。 其在晦、二日，則原乎定朔以得之。 列國之曆或殊，則稽於六家之術以知之。 此四者，皆治曆之大端，而預所未曉故也。
On the new moon of the tenth month (renshen) in Duke Zhao's twelfth year, the people of Yuan drove out Yuan Bo Jiao—a date that differs by one day from both the Lu and Zhou calendars. Zuo Qiuming recorded what he had heard. On the new moon of the eleventh month (jisi) in Duke Xi's twenty-second year, Song and Chu fought at Hong. The Zhou, Yin, and Lu calendars all place the event one day earlier—the date the men of Chu had reported. On the last day of the sixth month (dingsi) in Duke Zhao's twentieth year, the Marquis of Wei entered an alliance with Beigong Xi; On the new moon of the seventh month (wuwu), he then swore alliance with the people of the state. All three calendars place the events two days earlier—the dates the men of Wei had reported. Clearly the calendars of the various states cannot be forced into a single system. When a day in Du Yu's Long Calendar did not fall in its proper month, he altered the intercalary remainder in an effort to force agreement. Intercalary months might follow one another after barely ten months, or be separated by more than seventy—Du Yu's gravest mistake. When computed new moons run too early, one corrects them against solar eclipses recorded in the classics. When median qi runs too late, one clarifies the matter from winter-solstice entries in the historical commentaries. When a date falls on the last day of the month or on the second day, one must resort to true new moon to settle it. When the states' calendars diverge, one consults the methods of the six calendar schools to determine the truth. These four points are the great foundations of calendrical science—foundations Du Yu never grasped.
22
新曆本春秋日蝕、古史交會加時及史官候簿所詳，稽其進退之中，以立常率。 然後以日躔、月離、先後、屈伸之變，偕損益之。 故經朔雖得其中，而躔離或失其正； 若躔離各得其度，而經朔或失其中，則參求累代，必有差矣。 三者迭相為經，若權衡相持，使千有五百年間朔必在晝，望必在夜，其加時又合，則三術之交，自然各當其正，此最微者也。 若乾度盈虛，與時消息，告譴於經數之表，變常於潛遯之中，則聖人且猶不質，非籌曆之所能及矣。
The new calendar draws on Spring and Autumn eclipses, the timed conjunctions recorded in ancient histories, and the detailed observation logs of the historiographers; from the mean of their advances and retreats it establishes constant rates. It then applies joint adjustments for the sun's lodge motion, the moon's separation, advance and retard, and waxing and waning variation. Mean new moon may therefore hit the mean while lodge motion and lunar separation still miss their marks; If lodge motion and separation are correct but mean new moon misses the mean, comparison across generations will inevitably reveal error. The three quantities take turns as the governing standard, like scales held in balance: across fifteen hundred years new moons fall by day and full moons by night, and conjunction times agree as well—then the three methods naturally meet at their proper values. This is the subtlest achievement. When celestial degrees wax and wane with the seasons, warnings appear outside the standard numbers and irregular change hides in the obscure, even sages would not insist on certainty—such matters lie beyond calendar calculation.
23
昔人考天事，多不知定朔。 假蝕在二日，而常朔之晨，月見東方； 食在晦日，則常朔之夕，月見西方。 理數然也。 而或以為朓朒變行，或以為曆術疎闊，遇常朔朝見則增朔餘，夕見則減朔餘，此紀曆所以屢遷也。 漢編訢、李梵等又以晦猶月見，欲令蔀首先大。 賈逵曰：「春秋書朔晦者，朔必有朔，晦必有晦，晦朔必在其月前也。 先大，則一月再朔，後月無朔，是朔不可必也。 訢、梵等欲諧偶十六日，月朓昏，晦當滅而已。 又晦與合朔同時，不得異日。 」考逵等所言，蓋知之矣。 晦朔之交，始終相際，則光盡明生之限，度數宜均。 故合於子正，則晦日之朝，猶朔日之夕也，是以月皆不見。 若合於午正，則晦日之晨，猶二日之昏也，是以月或皆見。 若陰陽遲速，軌漏加時不同，舉其中數率，去日十三度以上而月見，乃其常也。 且晦日之光未盡也，如二日之明已生也。 一以為是，一以為非。 又常朔進退，則定朔之晦、二也。 或以為變，或以為常。 是未通於四三交質之論也。
Scholars of old who studied heaven mostly did not understand true new moon. Suppose an eclipse falls on the second day: on the morning of mean new moon the moon is still visible in the east; If the eclipse falls on the last day of the month, on the evening of mean new moon the moon is still visible in the west. That is how reason and number work. Some took this for a change in the waxing and waning crescents; others blamed loose calendar methods—adding to the new-moon remainder when the moon appeared at dawn of mean new moon, subtracting when it appeared at dusk. That is why official calendars were revised again and again. Bian Xin and Li Fan of the Han, noting that the moon is still visible on the last day of the month, sought to enlarge the obscuration-cycle head from the start. Jia Kui said: "When the Spring and Autumn Annals record a new moon or a last day, there must be a new moon and there must be a last day—the last day and new moon must fall before the month they belong to. If the head is enlarged first, one month will have two new moons and the next none—new moons would no longer be fixed. Bian Xin and Li Fan simply wanted to harmonize the cycle to sixteen days: waxing crescent at dusk, the last day extinguished—that was all. Moreover, the last day and conjunction-new-moon occur at the same moment and cannot fall on different days. " Reviewing what Jia Kui and his allies said, one sees that they basically understood the matter. At the junction of last day and new moon, beginning and end meet at the boundary where light is spent and brightness reborn; the degrees ought to be equal. When conjunction falls at midnight (zi), the morning of the last day is like the evening of new-moon day, and the moon is invisible at both. When conjunction falls at noon (wu), the morning of the last day is like the dusk of the second day, and the moon may be visible at both times. When yin and yang run slow or fast and orbit and clepsydra times diverge, the mean rate holds: if the moon is more than thirteen degrees from the sun and still visible, that is normal. On the last day light is not yet fully spent, just as on the second day brightness is already returning. Some took this as proof, others as disproof. Again, the advance and retreat of mean new moon yields the last-day and second-day cases of true new moon. Some treated these as anomalies, others as the norm. This shows a failure to grasp the doctrine of the four-three exchange of substance.
24
綜近代諸曆，以百萬為率齊之，其所差，少或一分，多至十數失一分。 考春秋纔差一刻，而百數年間不足成朓朒之異。 施行未幾，旋復疎闊，由未知躔離經朔相求耳。 李業興、甄鸞等欲求天驗，輒加減月分，遷革不已，朓朒相戾，又未知昏明之限與定朔故也。 楊偉採乾象為遲疾陰陽曆，雖知加時後天，蝕不在朔，而未能有以更之也。
Comparing the calendars of recent dynasties on a scale of one million parts, their errors range from as little as one part to as much as ten-odd parts short of a whole part. Checked against the Spring and Autumn Annals, the error amounts to barely one quarter-hour—over several centuries too small to account for waxing- and waning-crescent anomalies. Barely put into use, a calendar soon grew loose again—because its makers did not understand how lodge motion, lunar separation, and mean new moon must be solved together. Li Yexing, Zhen Luan, and others, seeking verification against heaven, kept adding and subtracting lunar parts and revising their systems; waxing and waning crescents contradicted one another—again because they did not understand the limits of dusk and dawn or true new moon. Yang Wei drew on the Supernal Icon calendar for his slow-fast yin-yang system; though he knew conjunction times ran late and eclipses did not always fall on new-moon day, he could not devise a remedy.
25
何承天欲以盈縮定朔望小餘。 錢樂之以為：「推交會時刻雖審，而月頻三大二小。 日蝕不唯在朔，亦有在晦、二者。 」皮延宗又以為：「紀首合朔，大小餘當盡，若每月定之，則紀首位盈，當退一日，便應以故歲之晦為新紀之首。 立法之制，如為不便。 」承天乃止。 虞𠠎曰：「所謂朔在會合，苟躔次既同，何患於頻大也？ 日月相離，何患於頻小也？ 」春秋日蝕不書朔者八，公羊曰：「二日也。 」穀梁曰：「晦也。 」左氏曰：「官失之也。 」劉孝孫推俱得朔日，以丘明為是，乃與劉焯皆議定朔，為有司所抑不得行。 傅仁均始為定朔，而曰「晦不東見，朔不西朓」，以為昏晦當滅，亦訢、梵之論。 淳風因循皇極，皇極密於麟德，以朔餘乘三千四十，乃一萬除之，就全數得千六百一十三。 又以九百四十乘之，以三千四十而一，得四百九十八秒七十五太彊，是為四分餘率。
He Chengtian proposed fixing the small remainders of new and full moon by solar and lunar anomaly. Qian Yuezhi objected: "Although conjunction times are calculated with precision, the month would too often run three long and two short. Solar eclipses would fall not only on new-moon day but also on the last day or the second day. " Pi Yanzong added: "At the era head, conjunction-new-moon should leave the large and small remainders exhausted; if one fixed the date every month, the era head would overflow and require retreating a day—the last day of the old year would have to serve as the new era's head. Such a rule would be awkward in practice. " He Chengtian abandoned the plan. Yu Jihe replied: "If new moon falls at conjunction and lodge positions already agree, why worry about too many long months? When sun and moon are separated, why worry about too many short months? " Eight Spring and Autumn eclipses omit the word "new moon." The Gongyang Commentary says: "The second day. " The Guliang Commentary says: "The last day. " The Zuo Commentary says: "The calendar office erred. " Liu Xiaosun calculated all eight to new-moon day and sided with Zuo Qiuming; he and Liu Chao both advocated true new moon, but the responsible offices blocked them and the reform was never adopted. Fu Renjun was the first to institute true new moon, yet he still held that "on the last day the moon must not appear in the east, and on new-moon day it must not appear as a western waxing crescent"—that at dusk the last-day moon should vanish. This was the same doctrine as Bian Xin and Li Fan. Li Chunfeng followed the Huangji calendar, which is denser than the Linde: multiplying the new-moon remainder by 3040 and dividing by 10,000 yields the whole number 1613. Multiplying again by 940 and dividing by 3040 gives 498 parts, 75, and a very-strong fraction—this is the quarter-calendar remainder rate.
26
劉洪以古曆斗分太彊，久當後天，乃先正斗分，而後求朔法，故朔餘之母煩矣。 韓翊以乾象朔分太弱，久當先天，乃先考朔分，而後覆求度法，故度餘之母煩矣。 何承天反覆相求，使氣朔之母合簡易之率，而星數不得同元矣。 李業興、宋景業、甄鸞、張賓欲使六甲之首眾術同元，而氣朔餘分，其細甚矣。 麟德曆有總法，開元曆有通法，故積歲如月分之數，而後閏餘偕盡。
Liu Hong found the ancient calendar's dipper fraction too large; over time it would run late against heaven. He corrected the dipper fraction first and then derived the new-moon method—making the denominator of the new-moon remainder unwieldy. Han Yi found the Supernal Icon calendar's new-moon fraction too small; over time it would run early. He adjusted the new-moon fraction first and then worked backward to the degree method—making the denominator of the degree remainder unwieldy. He Chengtian worked the quantities back and forth until the denominators for qi and new moon fit a simple rate—but then the stellar numbers could no longer share a common origin. Li Yexing, Song Jingye, Zhen Luan, and Zhang Bin sought a common origin at the head of each six-jia cycle for all methods—but the fractional remainders for qi and new moon are extraordinarily fine. The Linde calendar has its general method and the Kaiyuan calendar its comprehensive method; only when accumulated years equal the number of lunar parts do the intercalary remainders exhaust together.
27
考漢元光已來史官注記，日蝕有加時者凡三十七事，麟德曆得五，開元曆得二十二。
Reviewing historiographers' annotated records from Han Yuanguang onward, thirty-seven solar eclipses carry recorded times; the Linde calendar matches five, the Kaiyuan twenty-two.
28
其四沒滅略例曰：
The fourth section, summary principles on occlusion and extinction, states:
29
古者以中氣所盈之日為沒，沒分偕盡者為滅。 開元曆以中分所盈為沒，朔分所虛為滅。 綜終歲沒分，謂之策餘。 終歲滅分，謂之用差。 皆歸于揲易再扐而後掛也。
In antiquity the day on which median qi overflowed was called mo; when the mo parts were exhausted together it was called mie. The Kaiyuan calendar defines mo as the overflow of the mid-fraction and mie as the deficit of the new-moon fraction. The sum of a year's mo parts is called the divination remainder. The year's mie parts are called the usage discrepancy. Both ultimately derive from the Yijing divination procedure of counting once, counting twice, and then hanging the stalks.
30
其五卦候議曰：
The fifth section, the discourse on hexagrams and seasonal periods, states:
31
七十二候，原于周公時訓。 月令雖頗有增益，然先後之次則同。 自後魏始載于曆，乃依易軌所傳，不合經義。 今改從古。
The seventy-two seasonal periods derive from the Duke of Zhou's seasonal instructions. The Monthly Ordinances add somewhat to the list, but the sequence remains the same. Not until the Northern Wei were they entered into official calendars, following the transmitted Changes-orbit scheme—a scheme that does not accord with classical doctrine. The present calendar returns to the ancient practice.
32
其六卦議曰：
The sixth section, the hexagram discourse, states:
33
十二月卦出於孟氏章句，其說易本於氣，而後以人事明之。 京氏又以卦爻配期之日，坎、離、震、兌，其用事自分、至之首，皆得八十分日之七十三。 頤、晉、井、大畜，皆五日十四分，餘皆六日七分，止於占災眚與吉凶善敗之事。 至於觀陰陽之變，則錯亂而不明。 自乾象曆以降，皆因京氏。 惟天保曆依易通統軌圖。 自入十有二節、五卦、初爻，相次用事，及上爻而與中氣偕終，非京氏本旨及七略所傳。 按郎顗所傳，卦皆六日七分，不以初爻相次用事，齊曆謬矣。 又京氏減七十三分，為四正之候，其說不經，欲附會緯文「七日來復」而已。
The twelve-month hexagrams come from Meng's chapter-and-commentary: its reading of the Changes begins in qi and then illuminates human affairs. Jing Fang further assigned hexagram lines to the days of each term: Kan, Li, Zhen, and Dui each govern from the start of a solstice or equinox and each receive seventy-three eightieths of a day. Yi, Jin, Jing, and Da Chu each receive five days and fourteen parts; the rest receive six days and seven parts—applied only to divining calamities, omens, and the outcomes of fortune and misfortune. For observing the transformations of yin and yang, the scheme is confused and obscure. From the Supernal Icon calendar onward, all systems follow Jing Fang. Only the Tianbao calendar follows the Comprehensive Orbit Diagram of the Changes. Beginning with the twelve nodes, five hexagrams, and the initial line, then taking turns in governance until the top line ends together with median qi—this is neither Jing Fang's original intent nor what the Seven Summaries transmitted. According to Lang Yi's transmission, every hexagram receives six days and seven parts and does not govern in succession from the initial line—the Qi calendar is mistaken. Jing Fang also reduced the seventy-three parts for the four cardinal seasonal periods—a doctrine without classical warrant, devised only to harmonize with the weft-text phrase "after seven days, return comes."
34
夫陽精道消，靜而無迹，不過極其正數，至七而通矣。 七者，陽之正也，安在益其小餘，令七日而後雷動地中乎？ 當據孟氏，自冬至初，中孚用事，一月之策，九六、七八，是為三十。 而卦以地六，候以天五，五六相乘，消息一變，十有二變而歲復初。 坎、震、離、兌，二十四氣，次主一爻，其初則二至、二分也。 坎以陰包陽，故自北正，微陽動於下，升而未達，極於二月，凝涸之氣消，坎運終焉。 春分出於震，始據萬物之元，為主於內，則羣陰化而從之，極于南正，而豐大之變窮，震功究焉。 離以陽包陰，故自南正，微陰生於地下，積而未章，至于八月，文明之質衰，離運終焉。 仲秋陰形于兌，始循萬物之末，為主於內，羣陽降而承之，極於北正，而天澤之施窮，兌功究焉。 故陽七之靜始於坎，陽九之動始于震，陰八之靜始于離，陰六之動始于兌。 故四象之變，皆兼六爻，而中節之應備矣。 易爻當日，十有二中，直全卦之初； 十有二節，直全卦之中。 齊曆又以節在貞，氣在悔，非是。
The yang essence wanes along its path, still and without trace; it does not exceed its proper number—at seven it passes through. Seven is the proper number of yang—why inflate its small remainder to make thunder stir underground only after seven days? One should follow Meng: from the start of winter solstice Zhong Fu governs; one month's divination stalks—nine and six, seven and eight—total thirty. Hexagrams take earth's six and seasonal periods heaven's five; five and six multiplied yield one waxing-waning change, and after twelve changes the year returns to its beginning. Kan, Zhen, Li, and Dui govern the twenty-four qi, each hexagram line ruling in turn; at the beginning stand the two solstices and two equinoxes. Kan envelops yang within yin; therefore it begins at the northern cardinal, when faint yang stirs below, rising but not yet ascended. By the second month the congealing frost dissipates and Kan's course ends. The spring equinox emerges from Zhen, which first holds the origin of the myriad things and governs from within; then the mass of yin transforms and follows. At the southern cardinal the surge of abundance reaches its limit, and Zhen's work is done. Li envelops yin within yang; therefore it begins at the southern cardinal, when faint yin is born beneath the earth, gathering but not yet manifest. By the eighth month the brilliance of civilization fades and Li's course ends. At mid-autumn yin takes form in Dui, which first follows the waning of the myriad things and governs from within; the mass of yang descends and submits. At the northern cardinal the dispensation of Heaven's marsh reaches its limit, and Dui's work is done. Thus the stillness of yang-seven begins with Kan; the movement of yang-nine begins with Zhen; the stillness of yin-eight begins with Li; the movement of yin-six begins with Dui. Thus each transformation among the four images encompasses all six lines, and the correspondences at the median nodes are fully accounted for. The lines of the Changes correspond to days: the twelve median qi fall directly at the opening of each full hexagram; the twelve nodes fall directly at its middle. The Qi calendar again places the nodes at the second line and the qi at the fourth—this is wrong.
35
其七日度議曰：
The seventh section, the solar-degree discourse, states:
36
古曆，日有常度，天周為歲終，故係星度于節氣。 其說似是而非，故久而益差。 虞喜覺之，使天為天，歲為歲，乃立差以追其變，使五十年退一度。 何承天以為太過，乃倍其年，而反不及。 皇極取二家中數為七十五年，蓋近之矣。 考古史及日官候簿，以通法之三十九分太為一歲之差。 自帝堯演紀之端，在虛一度。 及今開元甲子，却三十六度，而乾策復初矣。 日在虛一，則鳥、火、昴、虛皆以仲月昏中，合于堯典。
Ancient calendars assumed fixed solar motion: one circuit of heaven marked the year's end, and stellar degrees were tied to the seasonal qi accordingly. The doctrine seems plausible but is wrong; over time the discrepancy only widens. Yu Xi recognized the problem. Treating heaven as heaven and the year as the year, he established a correction to track the drift: one degree of precession every fifty years. He Chengtian judged this rate too high, doubled the interval—and ended up with too slow a rate instead. The Huangji calendar split the difference at seventy-five years—a figure not far from the mark. Collating the ancient histories and the observation ledgers of the day-officials, one year's difference equals one thirty-ninth part excess by the universal method. From the epoch when Emperor Yao began the chronological reckoning, the sun stood at one degree within the Xu lodge. By the Kaiyuan jiazi year of our own time it has retreated thirty-six degrees, and the Qian divination stalks come full circle. With the sun at one degree Xu, the Bird, Fire, Mao, and Xu lodges all culminate at dusk in their proper median months—exactly as the Canon of Yao records.
37
劉炫依大明曆四十五年差一度，則冬至在虛、危，而夏至火已過中矣。 梁武帝據虞𠠎曆，百八十六年差一度，則唐、虞之際，日在斗、牛間，而冬至昴尚未中。 以為皆承閏後節前，月却使然。 而此經終始一歲之事，不容頓有四閏，故淳風因為之說曰：「若冬至昴中，則夏至秋分星火、星虛，皆在未正之西。 若以夏至火中，秋分虛中，則冬至昴在巳正之東。 互有盈縮，不足以為歲差證。 」是又不然。 今以四象分天，北正玄枵中，虛九度； 東正大火中，房二度； 南正鶉火中，七星七度； 西正大梁中，昴七度。 總晝夜刻以約周天，命距中星，則春分南正中天，秋分北正中天。 冬至之昏，西正在午東十八度； 夏至之昏，東正在午西十八度：軌漏使然也。 冬至，日在虛一度，則春分昏張一度中； 秋分虛九度中； 冬至胃二度中，昴距星直午正之東十二度； 夏至尾十一度中，心後星直午正之西十二度。 四序進退，不逾午正間。 而淳風以為不叶，非也。 又王孝通云：「如歲差自昴至壁，則堯前七千餘載，冬至，日應在東井。 井極北，故暑； 斗極南，故寒。 寒暑易位，必不然矣。 」所謂歲差者，日與黃道俱差也。 假冬至日躔大火之中，則春分黃道交於虛九，而南至之軌更出房、心外，距赤道亦二十四度。 設在東井，差亦如之。 若日在東井，猶去極最近，表景最短，則是分、至常居其所。 黃道不遷，日行不退，又安得謂之歲差乎？ 孝通及淳風以為冬至日在斗十三度，昏東壁中，昴在巽維之左，向明之位，非無星也。 水星昏正可以為仲冬之候，何必援昴於始覿之際，以惑民之視聽哉！
Liu Xuan, applying the Daming calendar's rate of one degree in forty-five years, would put winter solstice in Xu and Wei—yet at summer solstice the Fire lodge would already have passed culmination. Emperor Wu of Liang, adopting Yu Xiao's rate of one degree in 186 years, would locate the sun between the Dou and Niu lodges in the age of Tang and Yu—yet at winter solstice the Mao lodge would not yet have culminated. He attributed all this to the intercalary month falling between nodes, with the month slipping back and producing the apparent discrepancy. But the classic's full-year account cannot accommodate four intercalary months at once. Li Chunfeng therefore argued: "If Mao culminates at winter solstice, then at summer solstice and autumn equinox the Fire Star and the Xu Star would all lie west of the Wei cardinal. If Fire culminates at summer solstice and Xu at autumn equinox, then at winter solstice Mao would lie east of the Si cardinal. The offsets swing back and forth—they cannot prove precession. That argument, too, is wrong. We now divide heaven by the four images. At the northern cardinal, Xuanshao culminates at nine degrees Xu; at the eastern cardinal, Great Fire culminates at two degrees Fang; at the southern cardinal, Quail Fire culminates at seven degrees in the Seven Stars; at the western cardinal, Great Bridge culminates at seven degrees Mao. Summing the day and night clepsydra marks to approximate the celestial circuit and fixing stars by their distance from culmination: at spring equinox the southern cardinal stands at mid-heaven; at autumn equinox the northern cardinal does. At winter-solstice dusk the western cardinal lies eighteen degrees east of the Wu meridian; at summer-solstice dusk the eastern cardinal lies eighteen degrees west—an effect of orbital path and clepsydra reckoning. With the sun at one degree Xu on winter solstice, at spring equinox dusk one degree Zhang culminates; at autumn equinox nine degrees Xu culminates; at winter solstice two degrees Stomach culminates, and Mao's reference star stands directly twelve degrees east of the Wu meridian; at summer solstice eleven degrees Tail culminates, and the star after Heart stands directly twelve degrees west of the meridian. The four seasons advance and retreat without straying beyond the bounds of the meridian. Li Chunfeng judged this incompatible—he was mistaken. Wang Xiaotong also argued: "If precession carried the solstice from Mao to Bi, then more than seven thousand years before Yao the sun at winter solstice ought to have stood in Eastern Well. Well is the northernmost point—summer would dominate; the Dipper the southernmost—winter would dominate. Heat and cold would swap places—a thing that surely cannot happen. What is called precession is a joint drift of the sun and the ecliptic together. Suppose at winter solstice the sun stood in mid-Great Fire: at spring equinox the ecliptic would cross at nine degrees Xu, the summer-solstice path would lie even farther beyond Fang and Heart, and the distance from the equator would remain twenty-four degrees. Set the solstice at Eastern Well and the geometry works the same way. If the sun were at Eastern Well—still nearest the pole, still casting the shortest gnomon shadow—then the equinoxes and solstices would simply stay where they belong. With the ecliptic unmoved and the sun's daily advance unreversed, how could one call that precession? Xiaotong and Li Chunfeng held that at winter solstice the sun lies at thirteen degrees Dou, Eastern Wall culminates at dusk, and Mao stands to the left of the southeast corner—in the direction of daylight—where stars plainly are to be seen. Mercury culminating at dusk suffices as the mid-winter marker—why drag in Mao at first visibility only to mislead the people's eyes and ears?
38
夏后氏四百三十二年，日却差五度。 太康十二年戊子歲冬至，應在女十一度。
Over the Xia dynasty's 432 years the sun regressed five degrees. On winter solstice in Taikang 12, the wuzi year, the sun should stand at eleven degrees Girl.
39
書曰：「乃季秋月朔，辰弗集于房。 」劉炫曰：「房，所舍之次也。 集，會也。 會，合也。 不合則日蝕可知。 或以房為房星，知不然者，且日之所在正可推而知之。 君子慎疑，寧當以日在之宿為文？ 近代善曆者，推仲康時九月合朔，已在房星北矣。 」按古文「集」與「輯」義同。 日月嘉會，而陰陽輯睦，則陽不疚乎位，以常其明，陰亦含章示沖，以隱其形。 若變而相傷，則不輯矣。 房者，辰之所次，星者，所次之名，其揆一也。 又春秋傳「辰在斗柄」、「天策焞焞」、「降婁之初」、「辰尾之末」，君子言之，不以為繆，何獨慎疑於房星哉？ 新曆仲康五年癸巳歲九月庚戌朔，日蝕在房二度。 炫以五子之歌，仲康當是其一，肇位四海，復脩大禹之典，其五年，羲、和失職，則王命徂征。 虞𠠎以為仲康元年，非也。
The Documents read: "On the new moon of the last month of autumn, the chen did not assemble at Fang. Liu Xuan explained: "Fang is the lodge where the sun resides. Ji means to assemble. Hui means to come together. If they fail to align, a solar eclipse is implied. Some read Fang as the Fang star itself, but that cannot be right: the sun's position can be calculated directly. A careful scholar hesitates over such readings—why not simply read the text as naming the lodge where the sun stood? Skilled calendar-makers of recent times calculate that the September new moon in Zhongkang's reign had already passed north of the Fang star. The comment concludes: in the ancient text, the character for 'gather' and the character for 'compile' bear the same meaning. When sun and moon meet in auspicious conjunction and yin and yang are in harmony, yang keeps its place and holds its brightness steady, while yin displays its grace in modesty and hides its form. If the encounter turns violent and destructive, harmony is lost. Fang is the lodge assigned to the chen; xing is merely the name of a lodge—the principle is the same throughout. The Zuo Commentary speaks of "the chen at the Dipper handle," "Heaven's Grand Array blazing bright," "the opening of Descending Harvester," and "the end of the Tail star"—learned men cite these without hesitation. Why balk only at Fang? The new calendar places a solar eclipse at two degrees Fang on the gengxu new moon of the ninth month, guisi year, the fifth year of Zhongkang. Liu Xuan, reading the Song of the Five Sons, identifies Zhongkang as one of those princes. He took the throne over the four seas and restored Yu's institutions; in his fifth year, when Xi and He neglected their offices, the royal command went out to punish them. Yu Xiao dated the event to Zhongkang's first year—that is incorrect.
40
國語單子曰：「辰角見而雨畢，天根見而水涸，本見而草木節解，駟見而隕霜，火見而清風戒寒。 」韋昭以為夏后氏之令，周人所因。 推夏后氏之初，秋分後五日，日在氐十三度，龍角盡見，時雨可以畢矣。 又先寒露三日，天根朝覿，時訓「爰始收潦」，而月令亦云「水涸」。 後寒露十日，日在尾八度而本見，又五日而駟見。 故隕霜則蟄蟲墐戶。 鄭康成據當時所見，謂天根朝見，在季秋之末，以月令為謬。 韋昭以仲秋水始涸，天根見乃竭。 皆非是。 霜降六日，日在尾末，火星初見，營室昏中，於是始脩城郭、宮室。 故時儆曰：「營室之中，土功其始。 火之初見，期于司理。 」麟德曆霜降後五日，火伏。 小雪後十日，晨見。 至大雪而後定星中，日且南至，冰壯地坼。 又非土功之始也。
In the Discourses of the States, Duke Dan of Single says: "When the Horn of the chen appears, the rains end; when Heaven's Root appears, the waters recede; when the Trunk appears, plants and trees loosen their joints; when the Fourth Star appears, frost descends; when Fire appears, clear winds warn that cold is coming. Wei Zhao regarded these as Xia seasonal ordinances that the Zhou adopted. Reckoned from the opening of the Xia era, five days after the autumn equinox the sun stands at thirteen degrees Di, the Dragon's Horn is fully visible, and the season's rains may be considered finished. Three days before Cold Dew, Heaven's Root appears in the morning—the Seasonal Instructions say "then one begins to draw off the floodwaters," and the Monthly Ordinances likewise speak of waters drying up. Ten days after Cold Dew the sun reaches eight degrees Tail and the Trunk appears; five days later the Fourth Star appears. Hence the falling frost is the signal for hibernating creatures to seal their burrows. Zheng Xuan, relying on observations of his own day, placed Heaven's Root's dawn appearance at the end of the last autumn month and judged the Monthly Ordinances wrong. Wei Zhao argued that waters begin to recede in mid-autumn and are fully exhausted only when Heaven's Root appears. Both views are wrong. Six days after Frost Descent, with the sun at the end of Tail, Mars first appears and Encampment culminates at dusk—then palace and city walls may be repaired. Hence the seasonal warning: "When Encampment stands at mid-heaven, earthwork begins. Mars's first appearance marks the season for the minister of justice. The Linde calendar has Mars hiding five days after Frost Descent— it reappears in the morning ten days after Lesser Snow, and not until Greater Snow does the Fixed Star culminate—by which time the sun nears its southern limit, ice hardens, and the earth splits. That schedule is far too late to mark the start of earthwork.
41
夏曆十二次，立春，日在東壁三度，於太初星距壁一度太也。
In the Xia calendar's twelve stations, at Establishment of Spring the sun stands at three degrees Eastern Wall—one and a fraction degrees past Wall by the Taichu star table.
42
顓頊曆上元甲寅歲正月甲寅晨初合朔立春，七曜皆直艮維之首。 蓋重黎受職於顓頊，九黎亂德，二官咸廢，帝堯復其子孫，命掌天地四時，以及虞、夏。 故本其所由生，命曰顓頊，其實夏曆也。 湯作殷曆，更以十一月甲子合朔冬至為上元。 周人因之，距羲、和千祀，昏明中星率差半次。 夏時直月節者，皆當十有二中，故因循夏令。 其後呂不韋得之，以為秦法，更考中星，斷取近距，以乙卯歲正月己巳合朔立春為上元。 洪範傳曰：「曆記始於顓頊上元太始閼蒙攝提格之歲，畢陬之月，朔日己巳立春，七曜俱在營室五度。 」是也。 秦顓頊曆元起乙卯，漢太初曆元起丁丑，推而上之，皆不值甲寅，猶以日月五緯復得上元本星度，故命曰閼蒙攝提格之歲，而實非甲寅。
The Zhuanxu calendar's epoch falls in a jiayin year: on the jiayin day of the first month, at dawn's first light, new moon and Establishment of Spring coincide and all seven luminaries align at the head of the Gen corner. Heavy Li received his appointment under Zhuanxu; when the Nine Li corrupted the rites both celestial offices lapsed. Emperor Yao restored his descendants and charged them to oversee heaven and earth and the four seasons—a charge that continued through the courts of Yu and Xia. Named for the era that gave it birth, it is called the Zhuanxu calendar, but in substance it is the Xia calendar. Tang compiled the Yin calendar, resetting the epoch to the jiazi new moon of the eleventh month that coincided with winter solstice. The Zhou adopted it; a millennium after Xi and He, the dusk, dawn, and culmination stars had drifted by roughly half a lodge. In Xia reckoning the months that aligned with the nodes matched the twelve median qi, and so the Zhou kept to Xia seasonal ordinances. Later Lü Buwei acquired the system and made it Qin law. Recomputing the culmination stars and trimming to the nearest positions, he set the epoch at the jisi new moon of the first month of a yimao year, when Establishment of Spring coincided with conjunction. The Commentary on the Great Plan reads: "The calendar tradition begins at the Zhuanxu epoch, in the year Grand Beginning, Cycle Opening, Sheti-ge, the month Bi-Zhou, on the jisi day of new moon when Establishment of Spring fell—all seven luminaries together at five degrees Encampment. So the tradition runs. The Qin Zhuanxu calendar began its count in yimao; the Han Taichu calendar in dingchou. Pushed backward, neither yields a jiayin year; yet because sun, moon, and the five planets realign with the original stellar positions at the epoch, the era is named Embracing Darkness, Sheti-ge—even though it is not truly a jiayin year.
43
夏曆章蔀紀首，皆在立春，故其課中星，揆斗建與閏餘之所盈縮，皆以十有二節為損益之中。 而殷、周、漢曆，章蔀紀首皆直冬至，故其名察發斂，亦以中氣為主。 此其異也。
The Xia calendar places every chapter, obscuration, and era head at Establishment of Spring; when testing culmination stars and gauging the Dipper's position against intercalary surplus and shortfall, it treats the twelve nodes as the pivot for all adjustments. The Yin, Zhou, and Han calendars, by contrast, anchor every chapter, obscuration, and era head to winter solstice; their doctrine of "examining issuing and gathering" likewise privileges the median qi. That is the difference between them.
44
夏小正雖頗疎簡失傳，乃羲、和遺迹。 何承天循大戴之說，復用夏時，更以正月甲子夜半合朔雨水為上元，進乖夏曆，退非周正，故近代推月令、小正者，皆不與古合。 開元曆推夏時立春，日在營室之末，昏東井二度中。 古曆以參右肩為距，方當南正。 故小正曰：「正月初昏，斗杓懸在下。 」魁枕參首，所以著參中也。 季春，在昴十一度半，去參距星十八度，故曰：「三月，參則伏。 」立夏，日在井四度，昏角中。 南門右星入角距西五度，其左星入角距東六度，故曰：「四月初昏，南門正。 昴則見。 」五月節，日在輿鬼一度半。 參去日道最遠，以渾儀度之，參體始見，其肩股猶在濁中。 房星正中。 故曰：「五月，參則見。 初昏，大火中。 」「八月，參中則曙」，失傳也。 辰伏則參見，非中也。 「十月初昏，南門見」，亦失傳也。 定星方中，則南門伏，非昏見也。
The Xia Small Calendar is sparse, abbreviated, and partly lost, yet it preserves the traces of Xi and He. He Chengtian, following the Great Dai tradition, revived Xia reckoning and set a new epoch at the jiazi new moon of the first month at midnight on Rain Water—overshooting the Xia calendar in one direction and falling short of Zhou orthodoxy in the other. Small wonder that recent reconstructions of the Monthly Ordinances and the Small Calendar fail to match the ancient data. The Kaiyuan calendar, projected into Xia reckoning, places the sun at the end of Encampment on Establishment of Spring, with Eastern Well at two degrees culminating at dusk. The ancient calendar measured from the right shoulder of Shen, which then stood at the southern cardinal. Hence the Small Calendar says: "On the first month, at early dusk, the Dipper's handle hangs downward. The Dipper's ladle head rests against the head of Shen, marking the moment when Shen stands at culmination. In late spring the sun stands at eleven and a half degrees of Hairy Head, eighteen degrees from Shen's reference star; hence the text says, "In the third month, Shen sets." At Establishment of Summer the sun is at four degrees of Well, and at dusk Horn stands at culmination. The right star of South Gate enters Horn five degrees west of the reference point, and its left star enters Horn six degrees east of it; hence the text says, "On the fourth month, at early dusk, South Gate stands upright." Hairy Head then comes into view. At the fifth-month solar term the sun stands at one and a half degrees of Ghost Cart. Shen is at its greatest remove from the sun's path; measured with the armillary sphere, the body of Shen first becomes visible, while its shoulder and thigh are still lost in the haze. The stars of Room stand at culmination. Hence the text says, "In the fifth month, Shen comes into view." At early dusk the Great Fire stands at culmination. "In the eighth month, when Shen reaches culmination it is already dawn"—this passage too has been lost in transmission. When the chen star sets, Shen appears—not because Shen is at culmination. "On the tenth month, at early dusk, South Gate appears"—this passage too has been lost in transmission. When the Fixed Stars stand upright at culmination, South Gate sets—it is not a dusk sighting.
45
商六百二十八年，日却差八度。 太甲二年壬午歲冬至，應在女六度。
Over the 628 years of the Shang dynasty, the sun's precessional displacement amounted to eight degrees. In the renwu year, the second year of Tai Jia, the winter solstice should fall at six degrees of Woman.
46
國語曰：「武王伐商，歲在鶉火，月在天駟，日在析木之津，辰在斗柄，星在天黿。 」舊說歲在己卯，推其朏魄，迺文王崩，武王成君之歲也。 其明年，武王即位，新曆孟春定朔丙辰，於商為二月，故周書曰：「維王元祀二月丙辰朔，武王訪于周公。 」竹書「十一年庚寅，周始伐商」。 而管子及家語以為十二年，蓋通成君之歲也。 先儒以文王受命九年而崩； 至十年，武王觀兵盟津； 十三年，復伐商。 推元祀二月丙辰朔，距伐商日月，不為相距四年。 所說非是。 武王十年，夏正十月戊子，周師始起。 於歲差日在箕十度，則析木津也。 晨初，月在房四度。 於易，雷乘乾曰大壯，房、心象焉。 心為乾精，而房，升陽之駟也。 房與歲星實相經緯，以屬靈威仰之神，后稷感之以生。 故國語曰：「月之所在，辰馬農祥，我祖后稷之所經緯也。 」又三日得周正月庚寅朔，日月會南斗一度。 故曰「辰在斗柄」。 壬辰，辰星夕見，在南斗二十度。 其明日，武王自宗周次于師所。 凡月朔而未見曰「死魄」，夕而成光則謂之「朏」。 朏或以二日，或以三日，故武成曰：「維一月壬辰，旁死魄。 翌日癸巳，王朝步自周，于征伐商。 」是時辰星與周師俱進，由建星之末，歷牽牛、須女，涉顓頊之虛。 戊午，師度盟津，而辰星伏于天黿。 辰星，汁光紀之精，所以告顓頊而終水行之運，且木帝之所繇生也。 故國語曰：「星與日辰之位皆在北維，顓頊之所建也，帝嚳受之。 我周氏出自天黿； 及析木，有建星、牽牛焉，則我皇妣太姜之姪、伯陵之後逢公之所憑神也。 」是歲，歲星始及鶉火。 其明年，周始革命。 歲又退行，旅於鶉首，而後進及鳥帑，所以返復其道，經綸周室。 鶉火直軒轅之虛，以爰稼穡，稷星繫焉，而成周之大萃也。 鶉首當山河之右，太王以興，后稷封焉，而宗周之所宅也。 歲星與房實相經緯，而相距七舍； 木與水代終，而相及七月。 故國語曰：「歲之所在，則我有周之分也。 自鶉及駟七列，南北之揆七月。 」其二月戊子朔，哉生明，王自克商還，至于酆，於周為四月。 新曆推定望甲辰，而乙巳旁之。 故武成曰：「維四月，既旁生魄，粵六日庚戌，武王燎于周廟。 」麟德曆，周師始起，歲在降婁，月宿天根，日躔心而合辰在尾，水星伏於星紀，不及天黿。 又周書，革命六年而武王崩。 管子、家語以為七年，蓋通克商之歲也。
The Discourses of the States says: "When King Wu attacked Shang, Jupiter was in Quail Fire, the moon in Celestial Teams, the sun at the Ford of Split Wood, the chen in the Dipper's handle, and the star in Celestial Turtle." The older theory places the year at jimao; working out its crescent and dark phases, that was the year King Wen died and King Wu succeeded him as ruler. The following year King Wu took the throne; the new calendar fixed the new moon of first spring on bingchen—in Shang reckoning, the second month; hence the Book of Zhou says, "In the king's first year, on the bingchen new moon of the second month, King Wu consulted Duke of Zhou." The Bamboo Annals records, "In the eleventh year, gengyin, Zhou first marched against Shang." Guanzi and the Family Discourses, however, count it as the twelfth year—likely because they include the year in which he became ruler. Earlier scholars held that King Wen received the Mandate for nine years before he died; in the tenth year King Wu reviewed the troops at Mengjin; and in the thirteenth year he marched against Shang again. Calculated from the bingchen new moon of the second month in the first year to the day and month of the campaign against Shang, the interval is not four years. That account is incorrect. In the tenth year of King Wu, on the wuzi day of the tenth month by Xia reckoning, the Zhou army first took the field. Correcting for precession, the sun stood at ten degrees of Winnowing Basket—the Ford of Split Wood. At the first light of dawn the moon stood at four degrees of Room. In the Changes, thunder above Qian forms the hexagram Great Strength, and Room and Heart embody that image. Heart is the essence of Qian, while Room is the chariot-team of rising yang. Room and Jupiter in fact cross and align with one another, belonging to the spirit Lingweiyang; Hou Ji was conceived through this conjunction. Hence the Discourses of the States says, "Where the moon stands—the Horse of Chen, the agricultural omen—is where our ancestor Hou Ji received his heavenly alignment." Three days later comes the gengyin new moon of Zhou's first month, with sun and moon conjoined at one degree of Southern Dipper. Hence the text says, "the chen is in the Dipper's handle." On renchen the Mercury star appeared at dusk at twenty degrees of Southern Dipper. The next day King Wu left Zongzhou and encamped with the army. Whenever the moon is at new moon and still invisible, it is called "dead brilliance"; when it first shows light at dusk, it is called the "crescent." The crescent may appear on the second or third day; hence Completion of War says, "In the first month, on renchen, beside dead brilliance." The next day, guisi, the king set out in the morning from Zhou on the campaign against Shang. At that time Mercury and the Zhou army advanced together, from the end of Establishment through Ox Leader and Maid, crossing the void of Zhuanxu. On wuwu the army crossed Mengjin, and Mercury set in Celestial Turtle. Mercury is the essence of Zhiguangji, announcing Zhuanxu and closing the reign of the Water phase, and also the source from which the Wood Emperor arose. Hence the Discourses of the States says, "The positions of the star and the sun's chen all lie in the northern quadrant—what Zhuanxu established and Emperor Ku received in turn." Our house of Zhou issued from Celestial Turtle; and at Split Wood, where Establishment and Ox Leader stand—that is the deity on whom Duke Feng, descendant of Boling and nephew of our royal ancestress Tai Jiang, relied. That year Jupiter first reached Quail Fire. The following year Zhou first overturned the Mandate. Jupiter then retreated, lingering in Quail Head before advancing again to Bird Net—reversing its course to weave the destiny of the Zhou house. Quail Fire faces the void of Chariot Pivot, the region where grain is nurtured; the Millet star is bound to it, forming the great gathering-place of Completed Zhou. Quail Head lies west of the mountains and rivers; Great King rose there, Hou Ji received his fief there, and it became the seat of Zongzhou. Jupiter and Room in fact cross and align with one another, seven lodges apart; Wood and Water succeed and replace each other, spanning seven months between them. Hence the Discourses of the States says, "Where Jupiter stands—that is the allotted domain of our Zhou." From Quail to Teams stretch seven rows—the north-south measure is seven months. On the wuzi new moon of the second month the crescent first brightened; the king returned from conquering Shang to Feng—in Zhou reckoning, the fourth month. The new calendar calculates the full moon on jiachen, with yisi adjacent to it. Hence Completion of War says, "In the fourth month, when bright brilliance had already passed, on the sixth day, gengxu, King Wu performed the burnt offering at the Zhou ancestral temple." According to the Linde calendar, when the Zhou army first set out, the year was in Descending Harvest, the moon in Celestial Root, the sun in Heart with the chen conjoined at Tail, and Mercury setting in Star Record—falling short of Celestial Turtle. The Book of Zhou also records that King Wu died six years after the revolution. Guanzi and the Family Discourses count seven years—likely because they include the year of the conquest of Shang.
47
周公攝政七年二月甲戌朔，己丑望，後六日乙未。 三月定朔甲辰，三日丙午。 故召誥曰：「惟二月既望，越六日乙未，王朝步自周，至于酆」，「三月，惟丙午朏，越三日戊申，太保朝至于洛。 」其明年，成王正位。 三十年四月己酉朔甲子，哉生魄。 故書曰：「惟四月，才生魄。 」甲子，作顧命。 康王十二年，歲在乙酉，六月戊辰朔，三日庚午。 故畢命曰：「惟十有二年，六月庚午朏。 越三日壬申，王以成周之眾命畢公。 」自伐紂及此，五十六年，朏魄日名，上下無不合。 而三統曆以己卯為克商之歲，非也。 夫有効於古者，宜合於今。 三統曆自太初至開元，朔後天三日。 推而上之，以至周初，先天，失之蓋益甚焉。 是以知合於歆者，必非克商之歲。
In the seventh year of the Duke of Zhou's regency, the new moon fell on jiaxu of the second month, the full moon on jichou, and six days later came yiwei. The fixed new moon of the third month was jiachen, and the third day was bingwu. Hence Announcement to the Duke of Shao says, "In the second month, after the full moon, on the sixth day, yiwei, the king set out in the morning from Zhou to Feng," and "In the third month, on the bingwu crescent, three days later, on wushen, the Grand Guardian arrived at dawn in Luo." The following year King Cheng took the throne in his own right. In his thirtieth year, on the jiyou new moon of the fourth month, the crescent first formed on jiazi. Hence the document says, "In the fourth month, the crescent had just formed." On jiazi the Testamentary Charge was composed. In the twelfth year of King Kang, the yiyou year, the new moon of the sixth month fell on wuchen, and the third day was gengwu. Hence Charge to the Duke of Bi says, "In the twelfth year, on the gengwu crescent of the sixth month." Three days later, on renshen, the king charged Duke Bi with the host of Completed Zhou. From the campaign against Zhou to this point, across fifty-six years, the crescent phases, dark phases, and day-names all match without a single discrepancy. Yet the Triple Concordance calendar places the conquest of Shang in the jimao year—that is incorrect. A system that works for antiquity ought to agree with the present as well. From Taichu to Kaiyuan, the Triple Concordance calendar's new moons lag behind heaven by three days. Projected backward to early Zhou, it runs ahead of heaven—and the error grows ever worse. From this one knows that whatever agrees with Liu Xin's reckoning cannot be the year of the conquest of Shang.
48
自宗周訖春秋之季，日却差八度。 康王十一年甲申歲冬至，應在牽牛六度。
From Zongzhou to the end of the Spring and Autumn period, the sun's precessional displacement amounted to eight degrees. In the jiashen year, the eleventh year of King Kang, the winter solstice should fall at six degrees of Ox Leader.
49
周曆十二次，星紀初，南斗十四度，於太初星距斗十七度少也。
In the Zhou calendar's twelve stations, at the start of Star Record Southern Dipper stood at fourteen degrees—in the Taichu reckoning the star's distance from the Dipper was a little less than seventeen degrees.
50
古曆分率簡易，歲久輒差。 達曆數者隨時遷革，以合其變。 故三代之興，皆揆測天行，考正星次，為一代之制。 正朔既革，而服色從之。 及繼體守文，疇人代嗣，則謹循先王舊制焉。
The fractional rates of ancient calendars are crude; given enough time they inevitably drift out of alignment. Those who truly understand calendrical computation revise their methods as times change, so as to keep pace with heaven's shifts. That is why each of the Three Dynasties, at its founding, measured heaven's motion, corrected the star stations, and established a calendrical system for its age. Once the orthodox calendar was reformed, ritual dress and colors followed suit. When a dynasty passed peacefully from one ruler to the next, calendar officers succeeded one another in office and scrupulously maintained the institutions of former kings.
51
國語曰：「農祥晨正，日月厎于天廟，土乃脈發。 先時九日，太史告稷曰，自今至于初吉，陽氣俱蒸，土膏其動。 弗震不渝，脈其滿眚，穀乃不殖。 」周初，先立春九日，日至營室。 古曆距中九十一度，是日晨初，大火正中，故曰「農祥晨正，日月厎于天廟」也。 於易象，升氣究而臨受之，自冬至後七日，乾精始復。 及大寒，地統之中，陽洽於萬物根柢，而與萌芽俱升，木在地中之象，升氣已達，則當推而大之，故受之以臨。 於消息，龍德在田，得地道之和澤，而動於地中，升陽憤盈，土氣震發，故曰：「自今至於初吉，陽氣俱蒸，土膏其動。 」又先立春三日，而小過用事，陽好節止於內，動作于外，矯而過正，然後返求中焉。 是以及于艮維，則山澤通氣，陽精闢戶，甲坼之萌見，而莩穀之際離，故曰：「不震不渝，脈其滿眚，穀乃不殖。 」君子之道，必擬之而後言，豈億度而已哉！ 韋昭以為日及天廟，在立春之初，非也。 於麟德曆則又後立春十五日矣。
The Discourses of the States says, "The agricultural omen stands true at dawn, sun and moon reach the Celestial Temple, and the earth's pulses begin to stir." Nine days beforehand the Grand Clerk told Hou Ji, "From now until first auspiciousness, yang qi will rise together, and the earth's fertile moisture will begin to move." If the earth does not quake and the moisture does not shift, its pulses will swell with blight, and the grain will fail to sprout. In early Zhou, nine days before Establishment of Spring, the sun reached Encampment. The ancient calendar's distance to culmination is ninety-one degrees; on that day, at the first light of dawn, the Great Fire stood directly on the meridian; hence the text says, "the agricultural omen stands true at dawn, sun and moon reach the Celestial Temple." In the imagery of the Changes, when ascending qi reaches its limit, the hexagram Approach takes over; seven days after the winter solstice, the essence of Qian first returns. By Great Cold, at the midpoint of the earthly cycle, yang suffuses the roots of all things and rises together with the first sprouts—the image of wood still within the earth; once ascending qi has fully emerged, it must be extended and enlarged, and so the sequence passes to Approach. In the cycle of waxing and waning, the dragon's virtue is in the fields, receiving the harmonious moisture of the earthly way and stirring beneath the soil; ascending yang swells with force, and earth qi bursts forth in tremors; hence the text says, "From now until first auspiciousness, yang qi will rise together, and the earth's fertile moisture will begin to move." Moreover, three days before Establishment of Spring, Small Excess takes charge: yang prefers to restrain itself within while acting without—overshooting the mark in order to return to the center. When this reaches the northeast quadrant, mountain and marsh exchange their breath, yang essence opens the gate, split-shell sprouts break through, and the moment of grain-sprouting passes; hence the text says, "If the earth does not quake and the moisture does not shift, its pulses will swell with blight, and the grain will fail to sprout." The way of the noble person is to measure and verify before speaking—surely it is not mere guesswork! Wei Zhao held that the sun's arrival at the Celestial Temple fell at the very start of Establishment of Spring—that is incorrect. According to the Linde calendar it falls a full fifteen days after Establishment of Spring.
52
春秋「桓公五年，秋，大雩」。 傳曰：「書不時也。 凡祀，啟蟄而郊，龍見而雩。 」周曆立夏日在觜觽二度。 於軌漏，昏角一度中，蒼龍畢見。 然則當在建巳之初，周禮也。 至春秋時，日已潛退五度，節前月却，猶在建辰。 月令以為五月者，呂氏以顓頊曆芒種亢中，則龍以立夏昏見，不知有歲差，故雩祭失時。 然則唐禮當以建巳之初，農祥始見而雩。 若據麟德曆，以小滿後十三日，則龍角過中，為不時矣。 傳曰：「凡土功，龍見而畢務，戒事。 火見而致用，水昏正而栽，日至而畢。 」十六年冬，城向。 十有一月，衞侯朔出奔齊。 「冬，城向，書時也。 」以歲差推之，周初霜降，日在心五度，角、亢晨見。 立冬，火見營室中。 後七日，水星昏正，可以興板幹。 故祖沖之以為定之方中，直營室八度。 是歲九月六日霜降，二十一日立冬。 十月之前，水星昏正，故傳以為得時。 杜氏據晉曆，小雪後定星乃中，季秋城向，似為大早。 因曰功役之事，皆總指天象，不與言曆數同。 引詩云「定之方中」，乃未正中之辭，非是。 麟德曆，立冬後二十五日火見，至大雪後營室乃中。 而春秋九月書時，不已早乎。 大雪，周之孟春，陽氣靜復，以繕城隍，治宮室，是謂發天地之房，方於立春斷獄，所失多矣。 然則唐制宜以玄枵中天興土功。
The Spring and Autumn Annals records, "In the fifth year of Duke Huan, in autumn, a great rain-prayer ceremony was held." The commentary says, "It was recorded because the ceremony was held at the wrong season." For all sacrifices, the suburban rite is held at Awakening of Insects, and the rain-prayer ceremony when the dragon appears. According to the Zhou calendar, on Establishment of Summer the sun stands at two degrees of Turtle Beak. By clepsydra reckoning, Horn stands at one degree at dusk, and the Azure Dragon is fully visible. The proper time, then, is the start of Establishment of Snake—this is the Zhou ritual calendar. By Spring and Autumn times the sun had silently retreated five degrees; the month preceding the solar term still fell in Establishment of Dragon. The Monthly Ordinances places the ceremony in the fifth month; Lü's Annals, using the Zhuanxu calendar with Bearded Grain at Neck culmination, has the dragon appear at dusk on Establishment of Summer—ignorant of precession, and so the rain-prayer ceremony falls at the wrong season. Tang ritual, then, should hold the rain-prayer ceremony at the start of Establishment of Snake, when the agricultural omen first appears. If one follows the Linde calendar, thirteen days after Lesser Fullness the dragon's horn has already passed culmination—far too late. The commentary says, "For all earthworks, when the dragon appears the tasks must be finished and the work warned against." When Fire appears, put timber and earth to use; when Mercury stands upright at dusk, plant; when the sun reaches its term, finish. In the sixteenth year, during winter, they walled Xiang. In the eleventh month Marquis Shuo of Wei fled into exile in Qi. "Walling Xiang in winter was recorded because the timing was correct." Calculated with precession, in early Zhou at Frost Descent the sun stood at five degrees of Heart, and Horn and Neck appeared at dawn. At Establishment of Winter, Fire appears and Encampment stands at culmination. Seven days later Mercury stands upright at dusk, and timber and earthworks may begin. Zu Chongzhi therefore took the phrase "Ding is upright at center" to refer directly to eight degrees of Encampment. That year Frost Descent fell on the sixth day of the ninth month and Establishment of Winter on the twenty-first. Before the tenth month Mercury stood upright at dusk, which is why the commentary deems the timing correct. Du Yu, relying on the Jin calendar, places the Fixed Stars' culmination after Lesser Snow; walling Xiang in late autumn would then seem far too early. He therefore argues that labor and construction schedules refer only to celestial signs in general, not to precise calendrical reckoning. His claim that the Odes' line "Ding is upright at center" describes a moment before true culmination is incorrect. According to the Linde calendar, Fire appears twenty-five days after Establishment of Winter, and Encampment does not culminate until after Great Snow. Yet the Spring and Autumn records the ninth month as timely—is that not already too early? Great Snow is Zhou's first month of spring, when yang qi quietly returns; to repair walls and moats and maintain palaces at that season is to open heaven and earth's inner chamber—how much more is lost than by holding capital trials at Establishment of Spring! Tang institutions, then, should begin earthworks when Black Boar stands at culmination.
53
僖公五年，晉侯伐虢。 卜偃曰：「克之。 童謠云：『丙之辰，龍尾伏辰，袀服振振，取虢之旂，鶉之賁賁，天策焞焞，火中成軍。 』其九月十月之交乎！ 丙子旦，日在尾，月在策，鶉火中，必是時。 」策，入尾十二度。 新曆是歲十月丙子定朔，日月合尾十四度於黃道。 古曆日在尾，而月在策，故曰「龍尾伏辰」，於古距張中而曙，直鶉火之末，始將西降，故曰「賁賁」。
In the fifth year of Duke Xi the Marquis of Jin attacked Guo. Bu Yan said, "He will conquer."
